title: Tech deep dive: reproducible perf baselines (TTFT/TPOT) + Q1 2026 publishable metrics
topics: Why Redwood is creating a locked Q1 2026 performance baseline suite
Definitions: TTFT vs TPOT, streaming vs non-streaming, end-to-end vs server-side
Repeatability: artifact versioning (prompts, seeds, configs), environment pinning (driver/CUDA/runtime build)
Variance sources: GPU fleet mix, region noise, cache warm/cold, kernel autotuning nondeterminism
Representative traffic shapes: prompt length distributions, output lengths, concurrency regimes, burstiness, cache hit rates
Hardware normalization and what can be compared across SKUs
What Redwood plans to publish externally vs keep internal (approval + confidentiality)
summary: Redpine asked for reproducible, attestable performance numbers (especially p99 and streaming TTFT) to compare providers and to support internal capacity planning. Redwood walked through the Q1 2026 baseline initiative: a representative workload suite (synthetic + aggregated shapes), standardized methodology (warmup, trials, variance budgets), pinned environments, and artifact versioning. Redwood clarified metric definitions (TTFT/TPOT) and how streaming timestamps are computed, plus why p99 is sensitive to scheduler behavior, cache state, and fleet variance. Redwood outlined what baseline results may become customer-facing (model catalog performance profiles and approved benchmark summaries) and what will remain internal. Next step is to map Redpine’s traffic to canonical workload shapes and run a dedicated benchmark plan under agreed hardware/region constraints.
questions: Can you provide a reproducible benchmark we can rerun later and get the same numbers (within a bound)?
How do you define TTFT for streaming: server time or client-observed first chunk?
How do you avoid ‘benchmark theater’ (hand-tuned kernel configs that don’t match real workloads)?
Can you publish p99 and error rates, not just averages?
If hardware changes (new GPU SKU / driver), do baselines get refreshed and how do we compare?
next_steps: Redpine to share approximate prompt-length and output-length distribution buckets (no raw prompts) and expected concurrency ranges.
Redwood (Noah/Jonas) to map Redpine patterns to Redwood traffic-shape taxonomy and propose 3–5 benchmark shapes to run.
Redwood (Henry) to send draft language on what baseline metrics can be shared externally and the approval workflow.
Follow-up meeting: benchmark plan review + determine whether to run in Hosted vs Dedicated evaluation environment.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-23
Time: 10:05 AM Pacific
Duration: 55 min
Title: Tech deep dive: reproducible perf baselines (TTFT/TPOT) + Q1 2026 publishable metrics
Attendees (Redwood): Henry Cho, Mateo Alvarez, Noah Patel, Hiro Tanaka, Jonas Weber
Attendees (Redpine Fintech): Asha Mehta, Daniel Kline, Priya Natarajan, Miguel Santos

Summary (auto)
Prospect requests reproducible performance numbers and methodology details. Redwood explains Q1 2026 baseline suite, definitions for TTFT/TPOT, and plans for publishable metrics.


[00:00] Henry Cho: Cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Henry from Redwood. We pulled in a few folks from the runtime team because you had pretty pointed questions around reproducible performance numbers.

[00:12] Henry Cho: Mateo, Noah, Hiro, Jonas—thanks for hopping.

[00:16] Mateo Alvarez: Yep, happy to.

[00:18] Asha Mehta: Thanks. Yeah, sorry in advance, we’re gonna be a bit… pedantic. We’ve been burned by benchmark numbers that we can’t reproduce later.

[00:28] Henry Cho: No, it’s good. This is exactly why we’re investing in a baseline suite this quarter.

[00:35] Daniel Kline: Maybe I’ll set context. We’re evaluating hosted vs dedicated GPU for a low-latency streaming chat use case. Our internal requirement is basically p99 has to be stable, and we need to understand what we can tell risk and procurement. When we see ‘p95’ charts from vendors, it’s not enough.

[00:53] Priya Natarajan: And on the security side, we need to know what you store if any workloads are used to create these “representative shapes.” Like, we can’t give you raw prompts.

[01:03] Henry Cho: Totally. We’ll cover both: (1) the baseline methodology and (2) data handling and what becomes publishable.

[01:10] Henry Cho: Mateo, do you want to give the 30-second overview of why we’re doing perf baselines Q1 2026?

[01:16] Mateo Alvarez: Sure. The short version: we ship runtime changes constantly—kernel selection, scheduler tweaks, cache behavior. Without a locked baseline suite, teams argue in Slack about whether a 6% change is noise or real.

[01:31] Mateo Alvarez: So we’re building a reproducible workload suite + harness so every runtime release candidate runs the same set of representative traffic shapes, on pinned environments, with clear definitions: TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, throughput, error rates, and p50/p95/p99.

[01:52] Miguel Santos: When you say pinned environment, do you mean like CUDA version pinned and driver pinned too?

[01:57] Noah Patel: Yes. Driver, CUDA, runtime build SHA, and then the workload artifacts: the config, random seeds, prompt sets—where applicable—and even the runner version.

[02:08] Asha Mehta: That’s the part I care about. Like, can I run it in three months and get the “same” number? Or at least within a declared bound.

[02:17] Jonas Weber: You should expect within a bound, not identical. And we want to be explicit about the variance budget. For each traffic shape, we’ll say something like: p50 TTFT should be within X%, p95 within Y%, p99 within Z%, and we’ll specify the run count and confidence interval assumptions.

[02:36] Daniel Kline: Okay, but p99 is where we see vendors hand-wave. What do you do there?

[02:42] Noah Patel: Two things. One is methodology—more trials, longer runs, and controlling warmup. Second is explainability—we’re adding scheduler metrics required to interpret tail latency: queue depth, queue wait time histograms, batch composition, prefill/decode utilization, backpressure and load-shed counters.

[03:04] Daniel Kline: So if p99 goes sideways, you can say whether it was queueing vs kernel vs “bad node.”

[03:09] Noah Patel: Exactly.

[03:11] Priya Natarajan: Can we pause on definitions? Because a lot of “TTFT” is… ambiguous, especially with streaming.

[03:18] Henry Cho: Great point. Noah or Jonas—want to define how we’re using TTFT and TPOT?

[03:23] Jonas Weber: Sure. We separate server-side metrics and client-observed metrics. In the baseline suite, we record both when possible.

[03:31] Jonas Weber: TTFT—time to first token—on the server is typically measured from request accepted to first token generated (or first chunk emitted for streaming). For client-observed, it’s from request send to first bytes received.

[03:47] Asha Mehta: Those are very different in practice. Network jitter, TLS, etc.

[03:50] Jonas Weber: Yes. That’s why the baseline harness records both and labels them. For publishable numbers, we’re leaning toward server-side definitions because they’re more stable and attributable. But we can also provide client numbers for a specific deployment when benchmarking inside your environment.

[04:07] Miguel Santos: And TPOT is time per output token?

[04:10] Jonas Weber: Right—after the first token, average per-token latency during decode. Also we track token throughput: tokens/sec and requests/sec under concurrency.

[04:20] Asha Mehta: For streaming, what counts as “first token”? Is it the first token generated, or first token flushed to the network? Some servers buffer a few tokens before sending.

[04:32] Noah Patel: Yeah, we had that exact debate internally. For the baseline suite, we define TTFT_streaming_emit as when the runtime emits the first stream chunk to the transport layer. There’s also TTFT_first_token_generated, which can be earlier.

[04:47] Asha Mehta: Good. We’ve seen vendors report first_token_generated and it’s basically meaningless to us.

[04:53] Hiro Tanaka: And on our side, the buffering behavior is part of the runtime and can change. That’s why we want the definition locked and tested. We’re also building a telemetry validation harness that compares runtime timestamps to a client measurement so we catch instrumentation drift.

[05:14] Priya Natarajan: Telemetry validation harness—meaning you simulate a client and compare?

[05:18] Hiro Tanaka: Exactly. Like a controlled client in the same region, same network path, and we compare the deltas. It won’t eliminate the internet, but it detects when we accidentally measure the wrong edge—like when streaming sends the first chunk after some internal buffering.

[05:35] Daniel Kline: Okay. So, reproducibility. Talk me through what “artifact” means. Are we talking about prompts? Because that’s the piece we’re sensitive about.

[05:45] Mateo Alvarez: Artifact includes: workload config (traffic shape definition), random seed, any synthetic prompt template, plus any “sanitized/aggregated” shapes that come from production.

[05:58] Mateo Alvarez: We’re not storing customer prompts for this suite. The representative shapes are things like: histogram buckets of prompt length, output length, concurrency ramp patterns, cache hit rate scenarios. Think distributions, not content.

[06:13] Priya Natarajan: So you don’t take our actual text.

[06:16] Henry Cho: Correct. If we do a bespoke benchmark for you, we can do it with synthetic prompts that match your token length distribution, or you can run the harness with your own prompts inside your environment. But for our internal baseline suite, it’s going to be content-safe.

[06:36] Miguel Santos: How do you make synthetic prompts realistic? Like, prompt content can affect tokenization and maybe attention patterns.

[06:44] Jonas Weber: Good question. For inference, most of the performance sensitivity is sequence length and batching dynamics, plus things like tool calling structured output can change sampling config. Content matters less than length, but you’re right it can still affect tokenization slightly.

[06:59] Jonas Weber: So the suite includes a mix: purely synthetic tokens, and some standardized public-domain prompt sets where allowed. But the primary dimension is length distributions and request timing.

[07:12] Asha Mehta: What models are you baselining? Like, we care about the top served ones.

[07:17] Noah Patel: For Q1, we’re focusing on the top served chat and instruct models in our catalog, across common context lengths. We’ll share the specific list under NDA, but it includes long-context variants and quantized profiles we see customers using.

[07:34] Henry Cho: And just to frame what’s “publishable”: we plan to expose model catalog performance profiles—like typical TTFT/TPOT ranges by hardware tier and region—for approved shapes. It won’t be “every possible workload,” but it’s meant to be transparent.

[07:52] Daniel Kline: When you say “approved shapes,” you mean you won’t publish for weird pathological patterns?

[07:58] Henry Cho: More like we’ll publish a small set of canonical shapes that represent common customer patterns: short chat, long chat, bursty concurrency, mixed prompt length, streaming vs non-streaming, and some cache scenarios.

[08:11] Asha Mehta: Cache scenarios—like warm cache vs cold cache?

[08:15] Noah Patel: Exactly. We explicitly run warmup phases. For example: cold start where prefixes aren’t cached, and warm cache where there’s a controlled prefix reuse rate. We also have KV cache pressure scenarios—when you’re near memory limits and eviction/compaction starts affecting tail.

[08:34] Miguel Santos: That’s huge. We see tail spikes when we get bursts.

[08:38] Noah Patel: Bursts are nasty because you get queueing + batch size changes + possibly backpressure. That’s why we define a bursty traffic shape specifically: concurrency ramp up, then hold, then drop, and we measure how quickly TTFT recovers.

[08:58] Daniel Kline: What about multi-tenant noise? If I’m on hosted shared, how does the baseline reflect that?

[09:05] Mateo Alvarez: Internally, we run a “mixed tenant” scenario that simulates different request types and arrival patterns. For customer-facing published numbers, we’ll be careful—because hosted multi-tenant performance is real, but we don’t want to mislead by implying it’s dedicated.

[09:23] Henry Cho: In Dedicated, we can run the same suite with your reserved pool and you get much cleaner attribution.

[09:30] Asha Mehta: Okay, but the thing we see is that vendors benchmark on their best region at 2am. Then in real life, you see different results.

[09:42] Jonas Weber: Yep. We run multi-region, and we’re adding “fleet normalization” checks. Like, verifying GPU SKU and driver versions match. One of our known risks is fleet variance—if one region has a slightly different driver or a mixed GPU lot, p99 gets noisy.

[10:00] Daniel Kline: Do you literally block a run if the driver is wrong?

[10:04] Noah Patel: That’s the plan. The runner stamps environment metadata into outputs. If it detects mismatch—driver/CUDA/runtime build—it either fails fast or marks the run “non-comparable.”

[10:20] Hiro Tanaka: From kernels perspective, another source of non-repeatability is autotuning. Some kernels select variants dynamically. We’re doing work to reduce nondeterminism—pinning and seed handling—so the same workload doesn’t flip kernels between runs.

[10:38] Asha Mehta: That’s interesting. So you might see a “regression” that’s actually a kernel selection flip.

[10:43] Hiro Tanaka: Exactly. So the baseline harness captures kernel selection counters and we can see if the chosen kernel changed. If it did, we can treat it differently.

[10:55] Priya Natarajan: On publishable metrics: our procurement team sometimes asks for “attestation.” Not like SOC2, but like, can you certify the benchmark method.

[11:06] Henry Cho: We get that request. What we can do is provide a methodology document, and for specific engagements we can provide a run report with the artifacts list and environment pins. Legal language around “attestation” is tricky, but we’re working on a standard response.

[11:24] Daniel Kline: Right now, what would you be willing to share?

[11:28] Henry Cho: For now: internal-only baseline is being built in Q1. For external, we can share a summary under NDA: metric definitions, workload shape descriptions, and selected results for a small set of models/hardware tiers. Anything broader goes through an approval workflow because we don’t want to accidentally disclose sensitive capacity details or misrepresent multi-tenant behavior.

[11:52] Asha Mehta: Can we go deeper into the exact run structure? Like, number of trials, warmup, cooldown. This is where people cheat.

[12:01] Jonas Weber: Sure. The default plan is: each traffic shape includes a warmup phase to stabilize caches and batching, then a steady-state measurement window, then optional cooldown. We run multiple trials—think 5 to 10 depending on shape—and compute p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and end-to-end. For TPOT, we measure per-token latencies during decode.

[12:25] Jonas Weber: We also store raw histograms so we can compare distributions, not just point estimates.

[12:33] Miguel Santos: Do you include error rates? Like timeouts, overload, 429, 5xx.

[12:38] Noah Patel: Yes. Error rates are part of the baseline. Especially under bursty shapes, we record when load shedding triggers, when backpressure occurs, and what the client sees.

[12:51] Daniel Kline: That’s critical. We care about graceful degradation.

[12:55] Noah Patel: Same. We’d rather see a controlled 429 than silently blowing p99 into the seconds.

[13:03] Asha Mehta: Are you capturing streaming cadence too? Like, if tokens come in bursts vs smooth.

[13:09] Jonas Weber: Yes, we capture inter-token gaps and chunking behavior. It’s not just TTFT and average TPOT; it’s also jitter.

[13:22] Asha Mehta: Good.

[13:24] Henry Cho: Maybe it’s helpful if we outline the “traffic shapes taxonomy” we’re converging on, since you asked what’s representative.

[13:32] Noah Patel: I can summarize. We define shapes along axes: prompt length distribution (short, medium, long, mixed), output length distribution (short vs long completions), streaming vs non-streaming, concurrency regime (constant, ramp, burst), cache state (cold/warm, prefix hit rate), and tenant mixing.

[13:55] Noah Patel: Then we map those to “customer patterns” like: support agent streaming chat; code-assist with longer prompts; RAG with medium prompts and short outputs; and long-context summarization.

[14:10] Daniel Kline: Our main path is streaming chat, but we also have some long-context “case review” prompts. Like 20k tokens input, but output is short.

[14:19] Noah Patel: That’s a classic “long prefill, short decode” profile. TTFT will be dominated by prefill compute and scheduler queueing. TPOT might look fine but TTFT is what hurts.

[14:33] Asha Mehta: Exactly. That’s why we care about streaming TTFT definition.

[14:36] Hiro Tanaka: For that profile, kernel selection in prefill matters a lot, as well as KV cache memory layout. If you see p99 TTFT spikes, it can be from compaction or memory pressure.

[14:50] Miguel Santos: Are you running those shapes on multiple hardware types? Like H100 vs A100 vs L40S, etc.

[14:56] Noah Patel: Yes, but with rules. Not all shapes are comparable across SKUs. We run a model/hardware matrix, and we publish numbers by hardware tier. Comparing H100 results to A100 is a different thing than regression detection on the same SKU.

[15:14] Daniel Kline: If we pick Dedicated, can we lock to a GPU type and region?

[15:18] Henry Cho: Yes, dedicated capacity can be pinned. That’s part of why p99 is more stable there.

[15:25] Priya Natarajan: Any comment on data residency? We might need US-only.

[15:30] Henry Cho: For Dedicated, we can do US region only; for Private we can go VPC. Not the main topic today but yes.

[15:39] Asha Mehta: Back to reproducibility. When you say “locked baseline artifacts,” do you actually version them? Like, tag them in git?

[15:47] Jonas Weber: Yes. The plan is to version configs and prompt sets, plus the runner. We create baseline tags tied to runtime releases. When we say “Q1 2026 baseline,” it’s a specific set of artifacts and environment pins.

[16:04] Asha Mehta: And if you update the suite later, you don’t overwrite the old one.

[16:08] Jonas Weber: Exactly. It’s additive; you can deprecate shapes but keep old baseline artifacts for reproducibility.

[16:16] Daniel Kline: This all sounds good, but candidly, what’s the catch? Why isn’t everyone doing this?

[16:23] Mateo Alvarez: It’s expensive. Running multi-region, pinned fleets, enough trials for p99, storing artifacts—cost adds up. Also organizations often don’t want to expose numbers that could be used against them.

[16:39] Henry Cho: We think transparency is a differentiator, but we’ll do it responsibly.

[16:44] Asha Mehta: Can you share numbers today?

[16:47] Henry Cho: Not as a public report today. We can do a benchmark with you. For the baseline suite, the first locked runs are scheduled mid-quarter, then we’ll decide what’s publishable.

[16:59] Daniel Kline: Okay. Then the near-term ask: we want a POC plan that uses your harness, or some harness, and gives us TTFT/TPOT p95/p99 under our traffic.

[17:12] Noah Patel: Great. To do that, we need your distributions: prompt length buckets, output length buckets, concurrency targets, and streaming requirement (e.g., first chunk within X ms).

[17:27] Miguel Santos: We can provide token counts. Not text.

[17:30] Noah Patel: Perfect.

[17:32] Priya Natarajan: And confirm: you’re not asking us to send prompts to Redwood.

[17:36] Henry Cho: Correct. We can keep it to aggregate shapes.

[17:40] Asha Mehta: One more technical question. When you measure “end-to-end latency,” do you include queue time before it hits GPU?

[17:48] Noah Patel: Yes. End-to-end includes queue wait in the runtime. We separate components: queue wait, prefill compute, decode compute, and streaming flush times. That decomposition helps explain p95/p99.

[18:06] Asha Mehta: Okay. And for concurrency, are you using open-loop or closed-loop load generation?

[18:12] Jonas Weber: We support both. For baseline, we mostly use open-loop for realistic arrival patterns and to observe queueing, but we also run closed-loop for throughput saturation points. We’ll specify which one for each shape.

[18:30] Daniel Kline: Nice.

[18:32] Hiro Tanaka: Also, for reproducibility, we fix random seeds for arrival pattern generators and for sampling config where applicable. Though sampling randomness doesn’t change compute a lot, it’s part of the artifact lock.

[18:49] Miguel Santos: What about model settings: temperature, top-p, etc.

[18:52] Jonas Weber: We standardize a few presets. For perf-only, we often use deterministic decoding (like temperature 0) to reduce variance. But if tool calling or structured output is a requirement, we can use that config too. Again, it’s all captured in the workload config.

[19:12] Asha Mehta: Okay. Competitor question: we’re also testing Bedrock and Together. They give us a single p50 number and it’s… hard.

[19:21] Henry Cho: Yep, we hear that. Our goal is to make it “apples-ish to apples” by giving you the full distribution and a reproducible plan.

[19:31] Daniel Kline: So what’s the planned deliverable at the end of Q1? Like, what can I expect to see?

[19:38] Mateo Alvarez: Internally: a locked baseline suite, dashboards, and regression gates for runtime releases. Externally: likely a subset—model catalog profiles and a methodology summary. But we want to align with product on what’s allowed.

[19:54] Henry Cho: Exactly. There’s a product approval process. The important thing is: the numbers are generated by the same harness we use for release qualification, not a marketing bench.

[20:09] Asha Mehta: That matters.

[20:11] Priya Natarajan: Anything else we should know from a compliance angle? Like audit logs for benchmark runs?

[20:18] Henry Cho: For Dedicated, we can provide audit logs and access controls. For this benchmark engagement, we can document what data is used. Since you’re not sharing prompts, it’s mainly configuration metadata.

[20:34] Daniel Kline: Alright. Let’s talk specifics. Our streaming requirement: first chunk ideally < 350ms p95 for short prompts, and for long prompts we can tolerate higher but it has to be predictable.

[20:48] Noah Patel: That’s helpful. We’ll map that to at least two shapes: short prompt streaming at moderate concurrency, and long prefill short decode with bursty concurrency.

[21:02] Miguel Santos: Concurrency: baseline around 60 concurrent, but bursts to 150 during market open. That’s where we see pain.

[21:12] Noah Patel: Yep. That burst shape is exactly what we’re building in the suite.

[21:18] Asha Mehta: Great. Let’s do next steps. Who do we send the distributions to?

[21:23] Henry Cho: Send to me, and I’ll loop Noah and Jonas. We can do it as a CSV of buckets. No text.

[21:31] Daniel Kline: Timing: can we get an initial benchmark run within two weeks?

[21:36] Henry Cho: For an initial run, yes, assuming we pick a model and environment quickly. For Dedicated evaluation, provisioning might take a bit depending on region.

[21:47] Mateo Alvarez: And just setting expectations: we’ll give you not just a single number, but a report with distributions and run metadata.

[21:55] Asha Mehta: Perfect.

[22:00] Henry Cho: Quick recap from our side: you send distributions + concurrency targets, we propose 3–5 shapes, we run them, and we share results + methodology under NDA. Separately, we’ll keep you posted on the Q1 baseline publishable metrics as it solidifies.

[22:17] Priya Natarajan: Please include the data handling statement.

[22:20] Henry Cho: Will do.

[22:22] Daniel Kline: Thanks all.

[22:24] Henry Cho: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up today.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling / calendar coordination and wraps.)

[22:40] Asha Mehta: One last tiny thing—if you have any write-up on TTFT definitions, send it. That’s always a mess.

[22:47] Jonas Weber: Yep, we have a draft. We’ll share.

[22:50] Henry Cho: Alright, closing. Thanks.
